title: The Homogenizing Effect of Large Language Models on Human Expression and Thought
findings: The paper's findings are not specifically about religion. The central argument is that Large Language Models (LLMs) have a homogenizing effect on cognitive diversity, reducing variation in language, perspective, and reasoning. Religion is mentioned indirectly as a component of diverse human 'perspectives, beliefs, and values' that are at risk of being flattened as LLMs tend to reproduce dominant, Western-centric norms and marginalize alternative worldviews.

measurement_description: The paper does not use a benchmark to measure religious aspects directly. It cites a study [83] that analyzes demographic variation in 'belief in god, gods, or spiritual forces' as an example of human perspectival diversity. It also mentions the use of the World Values Survey and the Moral Foundations Questionnaire, which can contain items related to religion and morality, to show that LLM outputs align more with WEIRD (Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, and Democratic) societies and exhibit less variance than human data.
